questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a difference in species richness as a difference in biodiversity
questions.stem: One clinical note records that the hospital grounds carry 40 flowering plant species in the meadow strip and 8 in the car park. What does this comparison show about the meadow?

options.text: The meadow supports a wider variety of species than the car park
The car park supports more species, because hard ground favours wildflowers
options.misconception: assumes bare ground must support more wildflowers

options.text: Both strips are equally biodiverse, because both lie outdoors
options.misconception: treats any open ground as equally diverse

options.text: The meadow holds fewer species, because they are crowded into one strip
options.misconception: confuses the area of a site with its species richness

questions.explanation: Biodiversity at its simplest is the variety of species present, and 40 against 8 is a wider range in the meadow. Where the species sit within the site does not change how many kinds of organism live there.
questions.hint: Compare the number of different species.

questions.learningObjective: Place organisms at the correct trophic level from a feeding description
questions.stem: A pond where 400 water plants are eaten by 60 water fleas, which are eaten by 12 dragonfly larvae, appears in a clinician's note. Which description fits these figures?

options.misconception: picks the level with the largest count as the highest level

options.text: The plants are producers and the fleas are primary consumers
The dragonfly larvae are producers, because they feed directly on plants

options.misconception: labels a consumer as a decomposer without evidence

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a scheme for recording ecological succession over time
questions.stem: Bare ground on a disused hospital plot is colonised by mosses, then grasses, then shrubs over several years, according to a clinician's note. Describe how the sequence of change could be recorded properly.

answer.exemplar: The plot should be divided into fixed quadrats and each quadrat revisited at the same season each year, so that the same patch of ground is followed rather than a different patch each time. For every quadrat the recorder should note which species are present, how much cover each occupies and whether any seedlings have appeared, since seedling presence distinguishes the arrival of a new species from the spread of one already there. Bare ground should be recorded as a separate category rather than as zero cover, because the ground itself is the starting condition. The same quadrats should be followed for long enough to cover at least one full cycle of the plants being studied, and any disturbance to the plot should be noted, since clearing or excavation can restart the sequence.

questions.explanation: Succession is a change over time in what occupies a place, so the same ground must be followed under the same conditions each year. Fixed quadrats, recorded cover and seedling presence together show whether a species arrived new or merely spread.
questions.hint: Follow the same marked ground each time.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how interactions between two species can reduce one of them
questions.stem: The wildflower strip outside the clinic now has fewer daisies since bees were reintroduced, a clinician's note records. Explain how one species can reduce another in the same community.

answer.exemplar: Interactions between species can work in either direction depending on the resource involved. Bees and daisies compete for the same nectar and pollen, so more bees means each daisy receives a smaller share of pollination and produces fewer viable seeds, and the daisy population falls even though daisies are a favoured plant. The same pair of species could also interact beneficially, since a diverse strip of flowers gives bees a longer season of forage. The note therefore cannot assume that the presence of pollinators removes the plants, because what changes is the balance of competition between them.

questions.explanation: Species in a community interact through shared resources, so a change in one changes the conditions for the other. Bees and daisies compete for the same pollen, and the direction of the effect depends on which resource is limiting.
questions.hint: Think about the resource both species need.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise niche partitioning between two species in one place
questions.stem: Barn owls and tawny owls both hunt small mammals around the clinic, a clinician's note observes, but the barn owl takes mainly field mice while the tawny owl takes mainly voles. What does this show?

options.text: The two owl species are the same ecological niche with different names
options.misconception: treats a different prey choice as an identical niche

options.text: The two owl species occupy separate habitats, since they hunt different places
options.misconception: assumes different prey means different habitat

options.text: The two owl species partition the same niche by using different prey
The two owl species cannot compete, because they never meet
options.misconception: assumes competition requires the competitors to meet

questions.explanation: Niche partitioning happens when two species use the same place but divide the resources between them, and here the two owls separate by prey species. They still compete for the mammals that live in the same fields, so not meeting does not remove competition.
questions.hint: Look at how the two species divide their resources.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Link a loss of a natural filter to a downstream decline
questions.stem: A clinician's note records that a local stream's fish population fell after the reed beds upstream were cleared, and that the water became cloudier. Which explanation do these observations support?

options.text: The fish were caught by anglers, since fishing is common on that stream
options.misconception: assumes a cause with no evidence in the observations

options.text: The reeds provided shade that the fish needed to keep warm
options.misconception: invents a temperature effect not mentioned in the note

options.text: The fish left the stream because the reeds were cut at the wrong time
options.misconception: speculates about a reason not recorded in the note

options.text: Clearing the reeds removed the filter, so more silt reached the water

questions.explanation: Reeds trap suspended silt and their removal lets that material reach the water, which raises cloudiness and reduces the light and oxygen conditions that fish depend on. The fall in fish numbers following the clearing is consistent with that pathway.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design measurements capturing both the area and the biological cost of habitat loss
questions.stem: A meadow near the clinic is shrinking because a car park extension took one side of it, a clinician's note describes. Describe how the loss and its effects could be measured.

answer.exemplar: The boundary of the meadow should be mapped on a fixed scale before and after the change, so that the area lost is a measurement rather than an impression, and the same map should be used for the years that follow to see whether the edge keeps moving. Alongside the mapping, the recorder should count the species found in the remaining meadow and in an intact meadow of similar size elsewhere, because the number of species present is the most direct measure of what the loss has done. The comparison should also note whether the lost strip was a narrow edge or a whole habitat type, since a narrow strip of a common grassland removes less than a unique kind of ground, and any new road, fence or lighting that fragments the remainder should be recorded.

questions.explanation: Habitat loss shows up first as an area and then as a change in what lives in what remains, so both need measuring against a comparable site. Mapping the boundary and counting species in the remnant and in a reference meadow separates the effect of loss from ordinary year-to-year change.
questions.hint: Measure the area and count what is left.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how polluted runoff reduces the oxygen in a river
questions.stem: A clinic water sample ran cloudy after heavy rain, a clinician's note mentions, and the river's oxygen level fell after such an event. Explain the link.

answer.exemplar: Rainwater washing soil, road surfaces and animal waste into the river carries a load of suspended organic material and dissolved nutrients. Once in the water, bacteria decompose that material and consume dissolved oxygen, and a heavy input can strip the river of oxygen quickly enough to kill fish and invertebrates. Simultaneously the fine sediment scatters light, which stops plants in the river photosynthesising, so the water loses one of its own sources of oxygen at exactly the moment the oxygen is being used up. A cloudy sample after rain is therefore a visible marker of a large input of polluting material, not simply dirty water.

questions.explanation: Organic material entering the river is decomposed by bacteria, which consume dissolved oxygen, and the fine particles also block light so the river's plants make less oxygen of their own. A heavy input can therefore use up the river's oxygen faster than it is replaced.
questions.hint: Ask what decomposing material does to the oxygen.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a trophic cascade and the levels it runs through
questions.stem: A local lake lost its otters, then more fish appeared, and then more algae grew on the rocks, a clinician's note describes. Which process does this sequence illustrate?

options.misconception: describes a single-level effect rather than a cascade

options.text: A change in one species altering the population of a species it eats
options.misconception: describes a simple predator effect rather than a cascade

options.text: A change at one level working down through several levels of the food web
A change in one species altering the population of its competitors
options.misconception: describes competitive release rather than a trophic cascade

questions.explanation: A trophic cascade is a change that works down through the food web, and here removing otters released the fish from predation, which allowed the algae they ate to grow. The chain runs across three levels rather than staying between two.
questions.hint: Trace the effect through the food web.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Read a comparison suggesting that diversity buffers disturbance
questions.stem: Two meadow plots appear in a clinician's note: one with 14 plant species kept similar biomass through a drought, and one with 3 species whose biomass fell sharply. What does this suggest?

options.text: The species-rich plot was healthier because it had more biomass to start with
options.misconception: assumes a larger starting biomass explains the stability

options.text: Greater species variety appeared to buffer the plot against the drought
The three-species plot was healthier, because simple plots are easier to manage
options.misconception: confuses ease of management with ecological condition

options.text: The two plots behaved alike, because drought affects every meadow equally
options.misconception: ignores the differing outcomes recorded in the note

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a sampling scheme that can reveal biomagnification along a food chain
questions.stem: A clinician's note asks how to test whether mercury from a disused works is concentrating up the food chain in the local pond. Describe how the sampling should be arranged.

answer.exemplar: Samples should be taken from each level of the same food web rather than from different ponds, so that any increase in concentration is a property of the chain and not of where the sample happened to come from. In practice that means plants or algae, then invertebrates that graze them, then small fish that eat those invertebrates, and finally the larger fish that eat the smaller ones, with the water itself included as a reference level. Each sample should be recorded with its size and date, since mercury concentration rises with the age and size of an animal, and the tests should be run on the same tissue type in every group. A control site with no known contamination should be sampled in the same way at the same time, so that ordinary background levels can be told apart from any increase caused by the works.

questions.explanation: Biomagnification is a property of a food chain, so the sampling has to follow one chain from plants to the top predator, with a clean control site for comparison. Standardising tissue, size and timing keeps the comparison between levels fair.
questions.hint: Sample one chain from the bottom to the top.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the confounds that weaken a two-field comparison
questions.stem: A clinician's note proposes a trial of a new hay meadow treatment near the clinic, comparing two fields with different treatments. Explain the main flaws in the comparison as described.

answer.exemplar: The two fields differ in more than the treatment, because the note records them as differently sized and differently situated plots, so any difference in the number of species could come from the field itself rather than from the treatment. A trial of this kind needs the two fields to be as alike as possible before the treatment is applied, with the size, soil, drainage and previous use of each recorded, and the plots should be large enough and replicated enough that a single unusual corner of a field cannot stand for the whole. The note should also state how the species were counted, since a count made by one person in one field and another person in the other would introduce a difference of a different kind altogether.

questions.explanation: A comparison can only attribute an effect to the treatment if the two fields are alike in everything else, and different sizes and histories mean they are not. Recording the baseline conditions and using the same counting method in both fields removes those two sources of difference.
questions.hint: Ask what differs besides the treatment.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a way to distinguish succession from seasonal variation
questions.stem: A pond near the clinic has inbuilt-up over five years, with open water giving way to reedbed, a clinician's note describes. Describe how the change could be followed to test whether it is succession.

answer.exemplar: Succession is a directional change in community composition over time, so the pond should be followed in a way that separates a genuine progression from year-to-year variation in the weather. The recorder should fix a series of positions along a transect from the open water to the existing reedbed and revisit them each year at the same season, recording the depth of water, the sediment present and the species found in each segment, with a dated photograph from a fixed point for the record. The presence of new species should be recorded alongside a change in cover of existing ones, since succession usually brings new arrivals rather than only the spread of what is already there, and the years of observation should be long enough to cover more than one seasonal cycle so that a single dry or wet year is not mistaken for the direction of change.

questions.explanation: To show succession rather than ordinary variation, the same positions must be followed through time, with new arrivals distinguished from changes in cover. A fixed transect over more than one seasonal cycle keeps weather effects from being read as a trend.
questions.hint: Follow fixed points across more than one season.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how several interactions combine to shape a community
questions.stem: Grass by the clinic path is bare in a patch where people walk most, while grass two metres away is tall, a clinician's note records. Explain the interactions involved.

answer.exemplar: The bare patch is produced by more than one kind of interaction working together. Trampling is a direct physical effect in which people damage the plants as they pass, and it is strongest where people actually walk, which explains why the damage is concentrated on the path. Tread can also compact the soil, squeezing air from the spaces that roots need and slowing the return of water, so the grass recovers more slowly even where the treading is light. Light and water are then shared with the taller grass beside the path, and the trampled plants cannot compete for them. The result is a pattern of differential survival rather than a simple absence of grass.

questions.explanation: The bare patch is produced by direct damage, by the soil conditions that damage creates and by competition with the untouched grass for light and water. Several interactions reinforce one another, so the pattern is differential survival rather than simply no grass.
questions.hint: Consider damage, soil and competition together.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise temporal partitioning of a shared resource
questions.stem: Two plant species on a hospital bank flower at different times of year, a clinician's note observes, so that they rarely compete for pollinators. What does this describe?

options.misconception: treats sharing a place as sharing a full niche

options.misconception: confuses spatial overlap with competitive exclusion

questions.hint: Ask when each species uses the resource.

questions.learningObjective: Link nutrient enrichment to oxygen loss and a fish decline
questions.stem: After a fertiliser spill washed into a river upstream, fish numbers fell sharply while water plants increased, a clinician's note records. What explanation do these observations support?

options.misconception: invents competition between plants and fish for space

options.text: Fertiliser enriched the water, so plants grew and used up the oxygen

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a study of how clearance affects a ground-nesting bird
questions.stem: A hospital corridor of scrub was cleared for a car park extension, a clinician's note describes, and a colony of a ground-nesting bird lives nearby. Describe how the recorder should study the effect on the birds.

answer.exemplar: The recorder should first establish what was there before the clearance, because a bird that disappears after scrub is removed may have been breeding in it or may simply have been using it for shelter, and only the first makes the clearance responsible. Counts of breeding pairs, of nests found and of visits to feed should be made in the area that was cleared and in a comparable area of unaltered scrub, at the same time of year and for the same number of hours, so that the difference cannot be explained by effort. Because ground-nesting birds are easily disturbed, the recording itself should be kept to a fixed distance and the same hours each time, and the clearance area should be left alone for a year so that any return is not prevented by continued disturbance.

questions.explanation: Establishing the numbers before the clearance shows whether the birds were actually breeding there, and a matched comparison with unaltered scrub separates the clearance from ordinary variation. Fixed counting effort and fixed methods make the two areas comparable.
questions.hint: Count before and after, and use a matched area.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why algal growth lowers oxygen levels at night
questions.stem: An algal mat covers the rocks in a river downstream of a farm, a clinician's note mentions, and asks why oxygen levels fall at night. Explain the process.

answer.exemplar: The mat is a dense growth of algae, and living algae photosynthesise in daylight, taking in carbon dioxide and releasing oxygen, so during the day the river may carry more oxygen than it would otherwise. At night the photosynthesis stops while the algae continue to respire, consuming oxygen, and a dense mat contains a great many organisms doing so at once. If the mat is thick enough, the overnight loss of oxygen can exceed what the river gained during the day, and the oxygen level can fall low enough to deprive fish and invertebrates of what they need. This is why the worst oxygen readings typically occur in the small hours rather than at midday.

questions.explanation: Algae add oxygen by photosynthesis in daylight but consume it by respiration at night, so a dense mat can use up more oxygen overnight than the river gained during the day. The worst readings therefore come in the small hours.
questions.hint: Consider what algae do differently by day and by night.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a study comparing mercury in exposed and unexposed ponds
questions.stem: Testing whether a hospital's waste stream is adding mercury to the food web of the ponds downstream is the task a clinician's note sets. Describe how the test should be designed.

answer.exemplar: The design needs a downstream pond exposed to the hospital discharge and a comparable pond with no such discharge, and both should be sampled at the same times on the same dates so that seasonal differences in runoff cannot be mistaken for an effect of the discharge. Within each pond the same chain should be sampled from water and algae through grazing invertebrates and small fish to the large predatory fish, using the same tissue type in every sample, because mercury concentrates with the age and size of an animal as well as with trophic level. Every sample should be recorded with its length, weight and date, and the results should be compared level by level between the two ponds, since an increase that appears only at the top of the chain would have a different explanation from one that appears in the water itself.

questions.explanation: A test needs an exposed and an unexposed pond sampled in the same way and over the same chain, because mercury rises with both size and trophic level. Comparing level by level shows whether any increase starts in the water or appears only at the top.
questions.hint: Compare two ponds, and sample the whole chain in each.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the hidden differences that weaken a paired-bed comparison
questions.stem: One bed of wildflowers in a clinic garden was watered every morning and a second bed was not, and the two beds were only a metre apart, a clinician's note describes. Explain the problems with this comparison.

answer.exemplar: Two beds a metre apart share most of their surroundings, but not all of them, and the note gives no account of the differences that matter: the soil depth, the slope, how much sunlight each bed receives and whether one is closer to a building that shades it. The watering itself may also change more than water supply, since a permanently damp bed can host different insects and favour different plants, so the treatment is not a clean single factor. A sound comparison would replicate each treatment in several beds, randomise which bed receives which treatment in case a particular bed is simply better, and keep everything other than the watering the same.

questions.explanation: The two beds differ in more than watering, and the treatment itself changes several conditions at once. Replication and randomisation of beds, with everything else held the same, are what make the comparison able to support a conclusion.
questions.hint: Consider replication, randomisation and hidden differences.

questions.hint: Consider diversity within a species, not just between species.

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a biomass pyramid from a food web
questions.stem: A clinician's note records the following weights in a meadow food web: 300 kg of grass, 24 kg of voles and 3 kg of foxes. What does the pattern show?

options.misconception: states the ratio incorrectly and does not identify the pattern

options.text: Roughly a tenth of the energy passes to each level above
Each level holds the same number of kilograms after transfers
options.misconception: assumes material is fully converted between levels

options.text: The foxes outweigh the voles, so the figures must be reversed
options.misconception: invents an error where the data show a consistent pattern

questions.explanation: Across the three levels the figures fall by roughly a factor of ten each time, which is the familiar pattern of energy being lost between trophic levels. Only a small share of the energy at one level is converted into the next.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a study describing what has been lost at a changed site
questions.stem: A village pond beside the clinic was piped and filled in to make way for a car park, and a heron still visits the ditch beside it, a clinician's note describes. Describe how the recorder should study what has been lost.

answer.exemplar: The recorder should first establish what the site was, because the heron still visits the ditch, so the site has not simply become worthless, and without a before-picture the loss cannot be described in any meaningful way. Records of what was there, ideally from an earlier survey, aerial photographs or the accounts of people who used the place, should be assembled, and the species recorded from it listed. The same list should then be produced for a comparable pond elsewhere that still holds water, so the two can be compared species by species rather than in general terms, and the recorder should note the features of the lost site that a replacement could provide, such as open water of a particular depth and undisturbed margins.

questions.explanation: The size of a loss is only meaningful against a comparator, so the recorder needs a record of the site before it was changed and a matching intact site to compare it with. Comparing species by species makes the loss concrete rather than general.
questions.hint: Establish the before picture, then find a comparable site.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Trace a pollutant from water through a food chain into a person
questions.stem: A patient who eats local river fish twice a week has a blood mercury level above the reference range, a clinician's note records. Explain how a local pollutant reaches a patient's blood in this way.

answer.exemplar: Mercury released into a river is taken up by algae and small invertebrates, which are eaten in turn by fish, and because these organisms cannot excrete the metal efficiently its concentration rises at each step of the chain. A fish that has lived for years in the contaminated water therefore carries a far higher concentration than the water itself, and eating that fish transfers a large share of it into the human body in a single meal. The patient's blood level is thus a record of a food chain as much as of the fish, and the amount eaten and the frequency of eating both matter, which is why the note records both the fish and how often it is eaten.

questions.explanation: Mercury concentrates at each step of the food chain, so fish carry far more than the water they live in, and eating them transfers that into the body. The pathway runs through the food web, which is why the note records how often the fish is eaten.
questions.hint: Follow the metal up the food chain into the patient.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a sampling scheme comparing fish from two suppliers
questions.stem: Comparing mercury levels in fish bought from two different suppliers near the town is the task a clinician's note sets out. Describe how the sampling should be arranged.

answer.exemplar: Because mercury concentration depends on the age and size of a fish as well as on where it was caught, the samples from each supplier must be matched in those respects, so a small fish from one supplier is not compared with a large fish from the other. The recorder should specify the species, the length band and the tissue sampled for each fish, take a fixed number of samples from each supplier, and keep the two groups separated and labelled through the laboratory work. Each fish should also be traced to its catch area where that is known, because the pattern the note is testing is a difference between places rather than between species. The results should then be compared fish by fish within each size band, and any supplier whose fish have an unusually broad spread of concentrations should be examined for a mixed source.

questions.explanation: Mercury rises with the age and size of the fish, so the two suppliers' samples must be matched on species, size and tissue for the comparison to mean anything. Tracing each fish to its catch area then shows whether the difference is between places.
questions.hint: Match the samples on species, size and tissue first.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify why a single before-and-after measurement is a weak trial
questions.stem: One patch of a hospital courtyard was treated with a new anti-weed mulch and another was not, each measured once at the end of the summer, a clinician's note describes. Explain why the comparison is weak.

answer.exemplar: Measuring each patch once gives a single result for each, with no sense of how much the number would vary between patches or between years, so a difference between the two could easily be ordinary variation rather than the effect of the mulch. The note also gives no information about the two patches before the mulch was applied, so if they started with different weed cover the difference has already been decided. A usable design would need several replicate patches for each treatment, a record of the starting cover for every patch, the treatment applied at random to the patches, and repeat measurements through the season so that growth rates can be compared rather than single snapshots.

questions.explanation: One measurement of each patch gives no measure of natural variation, and no before-measurements mean a pre-existing difference cannot be ruled out. Replicates, starting measurements, randomised application and repeat readings are what the design needs.
questions.hint: Ask about replication, starting values and repeat readings.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a persistent succession from a single colonisation
questions.stem: Bare stones in a gravel pit beside the clinic are being colonised first by lichens and then by flowering plants, a clinician's note describes. Describe how the recorder should distinguish succession from a chance flush of plants.

answer.exemplar: The recorder should use fixed quadrats, placed over the bare stones and revisited at the same season each year, so that the same ground is followed rather than whichever patch happens to look richest. Each quadrat should record the species present, the cover they occupy and any seedlings, because the arrival of a new species is what distinguishes succession from the spread of plants already there. Because colonising plants often arrive in a single pulse and then fade, the record must run for several years so that a species present for one season is not counted as a permanent part of the community, and the dates of any disturbance such as flooding or excavation should be noted.

questions.explanation: Succession is a persistent, directional change, while a chance flush is a brief arrival, so the record must run for several years and follow fixed quadrats. Recording seedlings and cover distinguishes a new arrival from a species simply spreading.
questions.hint: Follow fixed quadrats over several years and record seedlings.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why one species can help in one setting and harm in another
questions.stem: Ivy on the clinic wall appears to benefit the wall lizards, while a thicket of ivy on the neighbouring fence appears to exclude them, a clinician's note records. Explain how the same plant can act in both ways.

answer.exemplar: The effect of a species depends on the resource that is scarce at the time. On the warm brick wall, the lizards can bask in whatever sun reaches them, and the ivy provides shelter, hunting perches and a damp place for invertebrates, so it adds to what the wall offers and the lizards use it more. On the fence, the same ivy grows so thickly that it covers the ground and the lower fence completely, which removes the bare ground, crevices and sunny patches the lizards rely on for basking and shelter. The plants are equivalent but the supply of space and heat is not, so what decides the outcome is which resource the ivy is using up.

questions.explanation: The same species can help or harm depending on whether it adds resources or removes them. On the wall the ivy adds cover and hunting places, while on the fence it takes up the bare ground and sunny patches that the lizards need.
questions.hint: Ask whether the plant adds a resource or removes one.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of a trophic cascade in a pond
questions.stem: Testing whether removing pike from a pond near the clinic changes the numbers of smaller fish and of the invertebrates they eat is the task a clinician's note sets. Describe how the test should be arranged.

answer.exemplar: Because removing pike changes one link of the food web and nothing else, the ponds used must be alike apart from that treatment, and each pond must be sampled before and after the change so that the effect can be separated from the ordinary year-to-year movement in fish numbers. Several ponds are needed for each treatment, with the removal ponds chosen at random from the eligible set, so that no single unusual pond carries the result. In each pond the same groups should be counted by the same method on the same dates: the pike, the small fish and the invertebrate groups they feed on, since a change in one group is what should be matched by a change in the next.

questions.explanation: A cascade test needs replicate ponds, random assignment of the removal and before-and-after counts of each link in the web. Counting the same groups by the same method shows whether the effect travels down the chain.
questions.hint: Use replicate ponds, random assignment and counts at each level.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain a pathway from contaminated ground to a drinking water source
questions.stem: A patient with persistent diarrhoea works in a vegetable market, a clinician's note records, and the note asks how run-off from the market could reach a well used for washing. Explain the pathway.

answer.exemplar: Rainfall on the market yard washes soil, animal waste and spilled cleaning chemicals into the drains rather than soaking away, because the yard is covered with concrete and cannot absorb what falls on it. From there the drain water enters a stream or soakaway, and if the well sits downstream of that point or draws from the same shallow groundwater, the same contaminants reach it. The risk is greatest after heavy rain, when the volume of polluted water entering the system is much higher than in dry weather, and it also lasts longer, since the contaminants continue to move towards the well long after the rain has stopped.

questions.explanation: Because paved ground cannot absorb the washings, rainfall carries them into drains and then towards any well or stream fed by the same water. The heavy-rain episodes deliver the largest and longest-lasting pulses of contamination.
questions.hint: Follow the water from the yard to the well.

options.misconception: rules out species composition as a factor in stability

The honest statement is a tendency with a qualification rather than a rule.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of mercury in fish from two waters
questions.stem: Comparing mercury in the town's lake fish with mercury in the fish of a nearby reservoir is the task a clinician's note sets out. Describe how the study should be set up.

answer.exemplar: The two waters should be sampled for the same species of fish in the same size range, because mercury concentration rises steeply with the age and size of the animal as well as with the length of the food chain, and a comparison of a small fish from one lake with a large fish from the other would measure that difference instead. The same tissue should be tested in both, and the number of fish taken from each water should be the same, with the fish from each lake sampled at the same season and, where possible, the same year, since the level in fish is not fixed from one year to the next. The location of every fish, its length and its date should be recorded, and the results compared as distributions rather than as single averages, since a lake with one very old fish and many young fish would otherwise look similar to a lake where every fish carries a high concentration.

questions.explanation: Comparing mercury between waters requires the same species, size range, tissue and season in both, otherwise the age of the fish explains the difference. Comparing the spread of results as well as the average shows whether a high average comes from a few old fish or from all of them.
questions.hint: Match species, size, tissue and season before comparing.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify the confounds in a survey using two different counters
questions.stem: One volunteer counted insects for an hour each morning along one route and a second counted for two hours each afternoon along a different route, a clinician's note describes. Explain what is wrong with this arrangement.

answer.exemplar: The two counters differ in four ways at once: the time of day they worked, the length of their counts, the route they walked and the person doing the counting, so any difference between the totals could be caused by any of them. Pollinator activity varies strongly through the day, with many species flying in the warm middle of the hours, so a morning count and an afternoon count are not comparable even if they lasted the same time. The comparison would need the same route, the same hours, the same counting method and either a design that swaps the volunteers between routes or one that assigns both to both, with the counts converted to a common rate per hour before they were compared.

questions.explanation: Changing the observer, the route, the time of day and the hours together makes any difference uninterpretable. Holding these constant, or swapping observers between routes, and converting to a rate per hour isolates what is being compared.
questions.hint: List everything that differs between the two counts.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design an investigation tracing the source of a mercury finding
questions.stem: Tracing the source of a mercury finding in patients who regularly eat fish from a particular lake is the task a clinician's note sets out. Describe how the investigation should proceed.

answer.exemplar: The question is whether the lake is the source, so the lake fish themselves must be tested first, at several sizes, since a lake fish carrying a high concentration identifies the water as the likely route and one with a low concentration points away from it. The patients' own blood results should then be compared with their reported intake, because mercury from a lake they do not fish cannot explain a high level in someone who never eats from it. A control group of patients who eat fish from elsewhere should be included for comparison, and the dietary history should be recorded in detail, including fish bought from shops, because a patient may attribute their intake to the wrong source. Where an industrial site lies upstream, its discharges should be checked against the lake's concentrations.

questions.explanation: Tracing a source means testing the suspected route first and comparing the patients' intake with their results, since people often misattribute which food they ate. A control group and a check of upstream discharges complete the picture.
questions.hint: Test the suspected route, then check what the patients actually ate.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a single-site before-and-after design cannot show
questions.stem: Birds were counted on a hedge before it was planted and again a year after, with no comparison site counted at all, a clinician's note describes. Explain what this design cannot show.

answer.exemplar: With only one site counted, any difference between the two counts could equally be a change in the birds themselves, in the weather, or in the observer's method, since there is nothing to compare against. A control site counted in the same way on the same dates is what would separate a change caused by the hedge from one that would have happened anyway, and counts on several dates at both sites would show whether any difference was consistent or just a single occasion. The note also needs to say how the birds were counted, since a change in effort between the two rounds would produce a change in the numbers with no ecological cause behind it at all.

questions.explanation: A single site before and after cannot separate the effect of the hedge from changes that would have occurred anyway, so a matched comparison site is needed. Repeat counts on the same dates at both sites show whether any difference was consistent.
questions.hint: Ask what the change would look like without the hedge.

options.text: No organism is a producer, because every chain here begins with an eater
options.misconception: ignores that sunlight enters the chain

questions.explanation: A producer is the organism that builds organic matter from an inorganic source, and only the clover does that, using sunlight and carbon dioxide. The rabbit and fox obtain energy by eating other organisms, so they are consumers at higher levels.
questions.hint: Look for the organism that makes its own organic matter.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a continuing succession from a single colonisation
questions.stem: A strip of former hospital land has gone from bare rubble to dense scrub in six years, a clinician's note describes. Describe how the recorder should check whether this is succession or just a single colonisation.

answer.exemplar: Six years of change could be one colonisation followed by nothing, or a continuing sequence, and the difference shows in whether new species keep arriving and whether the earlier ones persist. The recorder should therefore fix quadrats and revisit them at the same season every year, recording the species present, their cover and any seedlings, so that arrivals can be separated from spreads and declines can be seen. Because scrub itself changes the ground, by shading it out and by trapping litter, the site needs to be followed for several more years and the state of the soil and the light reaching the ground noted. Any disturbance such as a bonfire or clearance should be logged, since that can restart the sequence from bare ground.

questions.explanation: A single colonisation and a continuing succession look alike at one moment, so the record must show repeated arrivals and changes over several years of fixed quadrats. Noting soil and light changes, and any disturbance, explains the direction taken.
questions.hint: Look for repeated new arrivals over several years.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain a three-way interaction between plant, herbivore and predator
questions.stem: A single apple tree in a clinic courtyard shelters a large population of aphids, and birds that feed on aphids gather there rather than elsewhere, a clinician's note records. Explain the interaction between the tree, the aphids and the birds.

answer.exemplar: Three different interactions are running at once in the courtyard. The aphid population feeds on the tree's sap, so the tree and the aphids are in a relationship of herbivory that harms the tree and benefits the aphid. The tree also shelters the aphids from wind and rain, which protects them and lets their numbers build up, and the birds gather where the aphids are dense because that is where the food is. The birds in turn reduce the aphid population, so the numbers that settle at a level reflect the tree's contribution and the birds' predation acting on it at the same time.

questions.explanation: The tree is both food source and shelter for the aphids, and the birds follow the aphids because that is where their food is. The final aphid density reflects the tree's support and the birds' predation acting together.
questions.hint: Consider food, shelter and predation in turn.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish different niches within a shared location
questions.stem: A robin on the clinic lawn feeds on worms near the surface, while a blackbird takes fruit from the hedge above, a clinician's note observes. What does this show about their niches?

options.text: They occupy different habitats, since one is on the ground and one in the hedge
options.misconception: assumes a shared area means a shared habitat label

options.text: They compete directly for worms, which both species depend on
options.misconception: invents a shared resource that the note does not show

options.text: They use different resources in the same area, so their niches differ
They have the same niche, because both birds live on the clinic grounds
options.misconception: treats sharing a location as sharing a full niche

questions.explanation: A niche is built from the resources an organism uses and how it uses them, so two birds on the same lawn that take worms and fruit respectively occupy different niches. Sharing a place is not the same as sharing a way of living.
questions.hint: Compare what the two birds actually eat.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a change in soil chemistry affects which species thrive
questions.stem: A fern on the clinic wall thrives while a moss on the same wall has vanished, and the wall's mortar was repointed with a cement mix two years earlier, a clinician's note records. What does the note suggest?

options.text: The moss was removed deliberately, because it was harming the wall
options.misconception: invents a deliberate act with no evidence

options.text: The fern is a parasite on the moss, and has killed it off
options.misconception: labels a moss and a fern as parasitic, which they are not

options.text: The moss simply failed, and the fern is unrelated to the change
options.misconception: declines a link between two changes on the same surface

options.text: Cement pointing raised the wall's pH, and the moss was lost to that change

questions.explanation: Cement mortar is strongly alkaline compared with the lime mortar the moss had, so repointing changes the chemistry of the surface beneath it. The acid-loving moss is lost to that change, while the fern tolerates the higher pH, which fits what the note records.
questions.hint: Consider what the new pointing material did to the wall surface.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of the effect of hedge removal on insects
questions.stem: Testing whether the loss of a hedgerow beside the clinic reduced the insects visiting the flower bed along it is the task a clinician's note sets. Describe how the test should be arranged.

answer.exemplar: Since the hedgerow has already gone, the test has to use what remains of the comparison rather than a simple before-and-after. Several comparable flower beds should be chosen, some still backed by a hedgerow and some not, on matched aspects and soils, and insects should be counted on all of them with the same trap, the same effort and on the same dates. The counting should run for a full season, since insect numbers vary enormously between weeks and a short window could easily favour one group, and the same beds should be used throughout rather than reselected. The note should also record other differences between the beds, such as mowing and nearby planting, since those would otherwise be confounded with the hedgerow.

questions.explanation: With the hedgerow already removed, matched beds with and without a hedge must be compared with identical traps and effort over a whole season. Recording other differences between beds keeps the hedgerow as the only feature that explains the gap.
questions.hint: Compare matched beds, with and without a hedge, over a season.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a clear pond can still carry harmful pollutants
questions.stem: A pond beside the clinic holds clear water but few fish, and a pipe from the hospital car park discharges nearby, a clinician's note records. Explain how the water can look clean while the fish decline.

answer.exemplar: A pond can look clean and still be poisonous, because many of the worst pollutants are dissolved and leave no visible sign, whereas the materials that cloud water are often less toxic to fish. If the hospital discharge carries oil residues, metals or detergents, those enter the water invisibly and act on the fish directly through the gills and indirectly through the invertebrates the fish eat, whose numbers fall first. A useful check is therefore to have the water analysed rather than judged by appearance, to sample at several points including near the outfall, and to compare the results with a pond that has no discharge reaching it.

questions.explanation: Clear water can still carry dissolved pollutants, and the materials that make water cloudy are often less harmful to fish than the metals and detergents that leave no visible sign. A clear pond can therefore hold a toxic load.
questions.hint: Separate what looks dirty from what is actually harmful.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Identify a cascade running from a stocked predator downwards
questions.stem: Trout were stocked in a stream near the clinic, and then the numbers of small fish rose and the numbers of aquatic insects fell, a clinician's note describes. Which process does the record describe?

options.text: A change in one species altering the population of a species it eats
options.misconception: describes a simple predator effect rather than a cascade

options.text: A change in one species altering the population of its competitors
options.misconception: describes competitive release rather than a cascade

options.text: A change at one level working down through several levels of the food web
A change in the vegetation that spread to other groups of organisms
options.misconception: describes a habitat change rather than a food web cascade

questions.explanation: More trout meant more predation on the small fish, so their numbers rose and the insects they normally ate were eaten more heavily, so insect numbers fell. The effect has passed through two links of the food web, which is what makes it a cascade.
questions.hint: Follow the effect from the trout down to the insects.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a comparison of community evenness and recovery
questions.stem: One pond in a clinician's note has a dominant species making up 90 percent of the biomass while in another no species exceeds 40 percent, and the second recovered faster from a fish kill. What does this suggest?

options.text: The dominant species was the cause of the fish kill
options.misconception: treats an abundance figure as a cause of the mortality

options.text: A more even spread of species was associated with faster recovery
The uneven pond recovered faster, since dominance protects a community
options.misconception: reverses the reported outcome to fit a preferred rule

options.text: Both ponds recovered at once, since recovery depends on the pond alone
options.misconception: ignores the differing outcomes the note records

questions.explanation: Evenness matters as well as richness: where many species share the biomass, the loss of some individuals affects each species less severely than it does in a community dominated by one. The comparison supports the idea of evenness, though two ponds cannot settle it on their own.
questions.hint: Consider the balance between species, not just their number.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design an investigation of a new insecticide moving through a food chain
questions.stem: Checking whether a new insecticide used on the hospital grounds is reaching the local food chain is the task a clinician's note sets. Describe how the investigation should be set up.

answer.exemplar: The investigation has to follow the chemical up the chain rather than looking for it in one place, so the same groups should be sampled in order: the soil and grass where the insecticide is applied, the insects feeding on that grass, the small birds eating those insects, and the predators that eat the birds. Each group should be tested in the same way and at the same times, and the sequence of results across the groups is what reveals accumulation, since a fall in concentration at any step would suggest the substance is being broken down or lost. A comparable site where the insecticide is not used should be sampled in the same way at the same time, because background levels of these chemicals are rarely zero and only the difference from an untreated site can be attributed to the new use.

questions.explanation: Accumulation is revealed by the sequence of concentrations up the chain, so each level must be sampled with the same method and timing. A matched untreated site is needed because background levels of such chemicals are rarely zero.
questions.hint: Sample every level of the chain, plus an untreated site.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a two-hedge trial confounds and how to fix it
questions.stem: A trial of a different hedge mix at two sites on the hospital grounds planted one hedge in autumn and the other in spring, and counted each the following summer, a clinician's note describes. Explain what the trial can and cannot show.

answer.exemplar: Because the two hedges differ in both the mix planted and the season of planting, and because there is only one hedge of each kind, any difference in what was counted could come from the season, from the particular site, or simply from one hedge happening to do better than another. If the note is really about hedge mix, then the season of planting has to be the same for both and each mix needs several separate hedges at different places, not one. The counts should also be made the same way and at the same age of the planting, since young and established hedges support different insects, and the results from the two sites should be compared with each other rather than treated as final.

questions.explanation: The trial confounds the mix with the planting season and uses only one hedge of each, so no difference can be attributed to the mix. Each mix needs several hedges, planted at the same time and counted at the same age by the same method.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two hedges differ in more than the mix.
